Lyman Beecher
lī'mən bē'chər
n. (Lyman Beecher, 1775–1863, Connecticut and Ohio Presbyterian, revivalist, first president of Lane Theological Seminary)
English surname Beecher, a dweller by the beech trees; Lyman, from a place name, the meadow man.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Lyman Beecher trained under Timothy Dwight at Yale, pastored at East Hampton, Litchfield, and Boston, and in 1832 went west to be first president of Lane Theological Seminary in Cincinnati. He was the most energetic organiser of his generation: temperance societies, Sabbath observance, home missions, the campaign against duelling, and a vast programme for evangelising the Mississippi valley before Rome could settle it. He preached Taylor's doctrine of ability and was tried for heresy in 1835 by Joshua Lane Wilson of the Cincinnati presbytery on charges of denying original sin and teaching that regeneration is the sinner's own act; he was acquitted, appealed, and acquitted again, and the trial was one of the sparks of the Old School and New School division two years later. Eph 2:8 is the verse the charges turned on, that salvation is “the gift of God” (Eph 2:8).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines heresy as a fundamental error in religion, and a presbytery as a body of elders in the Christian church.

expand to see more

HER'ESY, n. A fundamental error in religion, or an error of opinion respecting some fundamental doctrine of religion.

PRES'BYTERY, n. A body of elders in the Christian church; a judicatory consisting of all the pastors of churches within a certain district.

TRIAL, n. The examination of a cause in controversy between parties before a proper tribunal.

Modern Corruption

The most effective organiser in American Protestantism, tried twice for the doctrine he preached.

expand to see more

Beecher is the point at which the New Haven theology became a movement rather than a lecture room. His energy carried Taylor's doctrine of native ability into the pulpits and societies of the West, and the revival technique followed it, because a doctrine of unimpaired power licenses any method that secures a decision. Eph 2:8 is the correction and it is brief: grace, through faith, “and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God” (Eph 2:8).

The dictionary does not treat Wilson's prosecution as mere ecclesiastical spite. Act 20:30 anticipates exactly this situation, men arising from within the body “speaking perverse things, to draw away disciples after them” (Act 20:30), and Rom 16:17 directs the church to mark the cause of division by its doctrine. That Beecher was acquitted twice is a judgment on the courts, not a vindication of the doctrine; the same assembly divided in 1837 over the questions his trial had raised. His organising instincts remain admirable and his theology of the will was the opening through which semi-Pelagianism entered American evangelicalism and stayed.

Usage

"“it is the gift of God” (Eph 2:8) — the point of the charges against him."

"“speaking perverse things, to draw away disciples” (Act 20:30) — the prosecution's text."

"“mark them which cause divisions” (Rom 16:17) — marked by doctrine, not temper."
